title: Writing: Summarising Implied Meaning
summary: How to read between the lines in summary tasks: analyse tone, word choice (connotation), figurative language, and put facts together to see the hidden argument.

p: Advanced summary needs implied meaning: what the author suggests without stating. You infer it from tone, word choice and context. This is vital for critical thinking and for editorials and literature.
Tone: 'Another brilliant idea from the management,' he said as the clumsy new policy was announced. Implied: the idea is terrible.
Word choice (connotation): 'The politician stated his position' (neutral); 'admitted his position' (reluctance, or a negative position); 'boasted about his position' (arrogance).
Figurative language: 'The new tax law is a bitter pill for the middle class.' Implied: unpleasant and hard to accept.

Putting facts together: 'The company reported record profits. The CEO's bonus rose 200%. Meanwhile staff were told there will be a pay freeze.' Implied: executives are rewarded at the staff's expense.

'The government's new "affordable housing initiative" will build 500 luxury apartments, starting at 100 million naira each. The Minister declared it a "victory for every Nigerian family."' The quotation marks around 'affordable housing' show doubt. The contrast between 'affordable' and 'luxury apartments at 100 million naira' is ironic. The Minister's words are left to stand against the facts. Implied summary: the programme is wrongly named and out of touch with ordinary Nigerians.

activity: Passage: 'The head prefect's new rule says all students must wear bright badges to "promote school spirit". Unsurprisingly, the badge company is owned by the head prefect's uncle. The badges are compulsory and must be bought at the school office for a "nominal fee" of two thousand naira each.' (a) What is implied about the prefect's motive? (To benefit his family financially.) (b) What do the quotation marks suggest? (The author doubts that the rule promotes spirit or that the fee is small.)

title: Structure: Idioms
summary: What idioms are, how they differ from proverbs, and ten common idioms and others with meanings and examples.

p: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be worked out from its words: 'It's raining cats and dogs' (raining heavily). A proverb is a complete sentence that gives advice or a general truth: 'Don't count your chickens before they hatch' (don't plan on something that has not happened). Mastering idioms is essential for fluency.

p: Break a leg: good luck to a performer (from theatre superstition). Bite the bullet: do something unpleasant and have it over with. Tighten your belts: spend less in hard times. See eye to eye: agree. Under the weather: unwell. The ball is in your court: it is your turn to act. Burn the midnight oil: work late. Cry over spilt milk: be upset about what is past. title: Comprehension: Critical Evaluation and Fallacies
summary: How to spot logical fallacies (hasty generalisation, ad hominem, false cause, bandwagon), bias (loaded language, omission, opinion as fact) and weak evidence.

p: Critical reading judges the quality, validity and persuasiveness of a text. You question the author's arguments, evidence and motives, tell fact from opinion and detect bias.

Hasty generalisation: a conclusion from too little evidence ('I met two rude people from that city, so everyone from there is rude'). Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument ('We should not listen to his views on climate change because he failed science at school'). False cause (post hoc): thinking that because B followed A, A caused B ('The new mayor was elected and then crime rose, so the mayor caused the crime wave'). Bandwagon: saying something is true because it is popular ('Everyone is buying this phone, so it must be the best').

Loaded language: words with strong positive or negative feeling ('the government's reckless scheme' against 'bold new scheme'). Omission: leaving out facts that go against the writer. Opinion presented as fact. Test evidence: is it relevant, sufficient and from a credible source?

'The "Clean City" initiative is a complete waste of taxpayer money. The councillor who proposed it, Mr Jones, is a known liar who was once fined for littering himself! Furthermore, my neighbour said the new bins are already broken. It is obvious that this project is a failure and should be scrapped immediately.' Ad hominem: attacking Mr Jones's character. Weak evidence: a single neighbour's remark (a hasty generalisation). Tone: angry and scornful, which reduces the writer's credibility.

activity: Name the fallacy: 'Everyone is buying this brand, so it is best' (bandwagon); 'He failed science, so ignore his views' (ad hominem); 'Two rude people were from that city, so all are rude' (hasty generalisation).

title: Vocabulary: Politics and Government
summary: Fourteen words of governance: legislature, executive, judiciary, democracy, autocracy, bill, act, veto, impeachment, electorate, franchise, gerrymandering, bicameral legislature, coalition and ideology.

p: The legislature makes laws (National Assembly, Parliament). The executive carries them out (President, Governor, ministers). The judiciary interprets laws (courts and judges). The separation of powers, with checks and balances, stops any one arm from becoming too strong.

title: Revision
summary: A summary of the term and a quick guide to four essay types, with a revision activity.

p: Twelve tenses (time and aspect); conditionals Types 0 to 3 (if + present, present; if + present, will; if + past, would; if + past perfect, would have); prefixes; the passive voice (to be + past participle); concord (compound subjects, proximity rule, collective nouns, there is/are, intervening phrases); adjuncts, conjuncts and disjuncts; simple, compound and complex sentences; prepositional phrases; idioms.

Two-syllable stress (nouns first, verbs second); vowel contrasts /ɪ/ and /iː/, /ʊ/ and /uː/, /æ/ and /ɑː/; using a dictionary and spelling rules. Paraphrasing poems and drama; summarising a talk; implied meaning; critical evaluation and fallacies.
